promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Physics on the move (motion, momentum and vehicle safety)
Powering Earth (energy resources, generation and the National Grid)

questions.q: How is the total stopping distance of a vehicle calculated?
questions.explain: Stopping distance is the sum of the thinking distance (during the driver's reaction time) and the braking distance (while the brakes act).

questions.q: What is the correct equation and unit for momentum?
options: p = mv, measured in kg m/s
p = ma, measured in kg m/s
questions.explain: Momentum equals mass multiplied by velocity and is measured in kilograms metres per second (kg m/s).

questions.q: Which factor affects a vehicle's thinking distance?
options: Whether the road surface is icy
questions.explain: Thinking distance depends on speed and the driver's reaction time, whereas brakes, tyres and road surface affect braking distance.

questions.q: A car of mass 1000 kg travels at 20 m/s. What is its momentum?
questions.explain: Using p = mv gives 1000 × 20 = 20 000 kg m/s.

questions.q: How do crumple zones, seatbelts and airbags reduce the force on a passenger in a crash?
options: They increase the time over which the passenger's momentum changes
They reduce the time of the collision
questions.explain: Because force equals rate of change of momentum, increasing the collision time reduces the force experienced.

questions.q: Which of the following increases a vehicle's braking distance?
options: A wet or icy road surface
questions.explain: Reduced grip on a wet or icy road means the brakes take longer to stop the car, increasing braking distance.

questions.q: An object of mass 2 kg has its velocity changed by 10 m/s in 0.5 s. What is the average force acting on it?
questions.explain: Force = change in momentum ÷ time = (2 × 10) ÷ 0.5 = 40 N.

questions.q: Why does drinking alcohol before driving increase stopping distance?
options: It increases reaction time, so thinking distance is greater
It reduces the grip of the tyres
questions.explain: Alcohol slows the driver's reactions, lengthening the thinking distance and therefore the overall stopping distance.

questions.q: Roughly what voltage is used to transmit electricity across the main transmission lines of the National Grid?
questions.explain: The National Grid transmits power at very high voltages of around 400 000 V (400 kV).

questions.q: Why is electricity transmitted at very high voltage in the National Grid?
options: To reduce the current, which reduces energy wasted as heat in the cables
To increase the current in the cables
To make the electricity travel faster
To increase the power delivered to homes
questions.explain: For a fixed power, higher voltage means lower current, and less energy is lost heating the transmission cables.

questions.q: What does a step-up transformer do in the National Grid?
options: Increases the current in the cables
questions.explain: Step-up transformers raise the voltage (and lower the current) for efficient transmission across the grid.

questions.q: Which of these is a renewable energy resource?
questions.explain: Wind is renewable, whereas coal, natural gas and nuclear fuel are all non-renewable resources.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a step-down transformer near homes?
options: To reduce the voltage to a safer level for domestic use
To increase the voltage for domestic use
To increase the current to dangerous levels
To store electrical energy for later
questions.explain: Step-down transformers lower the high transmission voltage to the safer mains voltage used in homes.

questions.q: What is the approximate voltage and frequency of the UK domestic mains supply?
questions.explain: UK mains electricity is supplied at about 230 V with a frequency of 50 Hz.

questions.q: What is a major environmental disadvantage of generating electricity by burning fossil fuels?
options: It releases carbon dioxide, contributing to global warming
It relies on the weather being sunny
It cannot be switched on quickly
questions.explain: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change.

questions.q: A transmission cable carries a current of 100 A and has a resistance of 5 Ω. How much power is wasted as heat in the cable?
questions.explain: Power wasted = I²R = 100² × 5 = 50 000 W.

questions.q: What type of star is our Sun, and what process powers it?
options: A main sequence star powered by the fusion of hydrogen into helium
A red giant powered by the fission of uranium
A white dwarf powered by burning coal
A supernova powered by the fusion of iron
questions.explain: The Sun is a stable main sequence star that releases energy by fusing hydrogen nuclei into helium.

questions.q: Light from distant galaxies is shifted towards the red (longer wavelength) end of the spectrum. What does this red-shift suggest?
options: The universe is expanding, with galaxies moving away from us
Distant galaxies are moving towards us
Light slows down as it crosses space
questions.explain: Red-shift shows galaxies are receding, and more distant ones recede faster, supporting an expanding universe and the Big Bang theory.

questions.q: From what does a star first begin to form?
options: A cloud of gas and dust (a nebula)
questions.explain: Stars form when gravity pulls together a cloud of gas and dust (a nebula) to create a protostar.

questions.q: A satellite moves in a stable circular orbit at constant speed. Why is it still accelerating?
options: Its direction, and therefore its velocity, is continually changing
There is no force acting on it
questions.explain: Gravity provides a force towards the centre that constantly changes the satellite's direction, so its velocity changes and it accelerates even at constant speed.
